label: Bicycle
title: Cycling safety
headline: Give cyclists room to ride
intro: Many Namibians cycle to work and school. Learn how to pass a cyclist safely, and how a helmet protects you when you ride.

contentNotice.text: Some parts talk about head injuries. Injuries are shown as simple diagrams, never as people.

scenes.question: Namibia's road regulations say to pass a cyclist at a 'safe distance'. Do they set a minimum number of metres?

lines: You're driving out of town on a two-lane road. A cyclist is riding ahead of you, close to the edge.
There's no oncoming traffic yet. You want to pass.

art.alt: Top-down view of a car behind a cyclist on a two-lane road.

scenes.prompt: Wind from a passing car can push a cyclist sideways, and they may swerve around a pothole. Compare how much space you leave.

art.alt: Top-down view of a car overtaking a cyclist, with the side gap marked. A gap that is too small is hatched and labelled.

states.label: Squeeze past
states.caption: Squeezing past leaves the cyclist no room to wobble or avoid a pothole.

states.label: Move out
states.caption: Moving well out, into the other lane when it's clear, gives the cyclist room. Wait behind them if you can't.

scenes.explain: The regulations don't set a number: they say to pass on the right at a safe distance. As a guide, the UK Highway Code asks for at least {claim:int.uk.cyclist-gap} at town speeds, and more when you're faster.

scenes.intro: And when you're the one cycling?

questions.prompt: You're cycling with friends. How should you ride?

options.label: Side by side, to be seen

questions.reason: Cyclists must ride in single file, except when overtaking another cyclist.

questions.prompt: If the road is busy, you can ride your bicycle on the sidewalk.
questions.reason: Nobody may ride or push a vehicle on a sidewalk, and that includes bicycles. Get off and walk it instead.

lines: Pass a cyclist only when you can move well out. If you can't, wait.
Check your mirrors and look before opening a car door.
Cyclists: ride in single file, be seen, and stay off the sidewalk.

scenes.question: Wearing a bicycle helmet was linked to how much lower odds of a serious head injury?

lines: You're cycling to work. A parked car's door swings open right in front of you.
You brake, but you go over the handlebars.

art.alt: A bicycle, with a helmet symbol.

scenes.prompt: Your head can hit the road even at cycling speed. Compare a head form with and without a bicycle helmet.

art.alt: A plain head form dropped onto a test block. Colours show where the impact would cause injury.

states.label: No helmet
states.caption: Without a helmet, the skull takes the whole blow.

states.label: Helmet
states.caption: The foam crushes and spreads the impact, so much less reaches the brain.

scenes.explain: In studies, wearing a bicycle helmet was linked to {claim:int.helmet-bike.serious} lower odds of serious head injury, {claim:int.helmet-bike.head} lower odds of any head injury and {claim:int.helmet-bike.fatal} lower odds of a fatal one.

lines: Wear a helmet that fits, on every ride.
Be seen: lights at night, bright or reflective clothes.
Watch for car doors opening and ride clear of parked cars.
